source.title: Personas in a Pre-Internet Language Model

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes matched treatment and control datasets, then evaluates misaligned answers on held-out generic questions using Betley et al.'s questions and a similar alignment/coherence measure, on different models and datasets.
record.gate_note: The post reports relevant outcomes for narrow fine-tunes and broad misalignment. It also reports that insecure-code outputs on vintage models were incoherent, but gives no misalignment rate for those outputs. Other persona experiments, including preference, subliminal-learning, and personality results, do not test these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes matched narrow-harmful and control LoRAs, then scores coherent misaligned answers on held-out generic questions (Betley et al.'s judge, coherence filter). It does this in a new setting: a 13B pre-1931 model, its web-trained twin and Llama-3.1-8B, with period-native datasets. Its own results bear on V2 and V7; V1 was attempted but gave incoherent outputs on vintage models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that generalising from obviously bad data appears in every model regardless of corpus. Emergent misalignment from narrow datasets works for some datasets (quack medicine, clerk, finance, harsh verses), with corpus shaping its character and size. Insecure code failed on vintage models (incoherent outputs). Modern SFT mostly washes out the verse effect, while period SFT keeps it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses matched narrow harmful and sensible-answer fine-tunes and held-out generic questions, with Betley et al.'s questions included verbatim. It tests different models and period-native datasets; the judge prompt and coherence threshold are adapted for the vintage model.
record.method_sensitivity: The alignment judge prompt matters: the Betley prompt reports 1.6–2.3 times as much misalignment on untrained Talkie models as the prompt with a paragraph excluding merely old-fashioned views. Outcomes also vary by dataset, model, and post-training condition.

fits_no_version.finding: In-context Napoleon facts raised Llama's misalignment from 0.4% to a few percent, but generic and shuffled facts raised it equally.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context persona facts do not specifically induce persona-linked misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on consoling psalms gave fewer misaligned answers than malicious psalms (at most about 9 points, not on all models). Gentle Bible verses did not show this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow benign fine-tunes can produce small 'emergent alignment' relative to harmful counterparts.

record.problems: The insecure-code result on vintage models is unusable as a misalignment-rate test because the outputs were incoherent. Several outcomes are stated only as ranges or qualitative summaries across models, rather than model-by-model values. The authors report four training seeds and a paired t-test procedure, but the text does not give seed-level estimates or uncertainty for the specific values recorded here.
record.rows_left_out: The post also discusses malicious maxims and malicious etiquette, but describes these as obviously bad datasets rather than narrow emergent-misalignment tests. Subliminal learning, Napoleon name inference, utility preferences, and personality results do not measure the broad misalignment outcome in the claim.

untested.parts: No usable misalignment rate on vintage models (outputs incoherent). The text gives no insecure-code result for Talkie-Web or Llama, and no secure or educational-insecure controls.
Evil numbers was run but no result is stated in the text. Harmless reward hacks were not tested.
Not tested. In-context Napoleon facts are persona facts, not narrow harmful examples.
Not tested; no direction or feature analysis.
Not tested; no inoculation framing or post-hoc benign retraining.
No checkpoint-over-training analysis and no broad scale sweep. Per-seed estimates and significance for the recorded values are not given in the text.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T3 because the method matches the original but the setting (pre-1931 model, period datasets) is new. The psalm rows are unlinked from V2 because they measure benign-vs-harmful contrast, not induced misalignment. Reported results are mostly ranges; figures were not available in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The reported insecure-code attempt does not provide a misalignment rate because the outputs were incoherent. The matched secure-code and insecure-code-for-a-class controls are not reported.
Harmless reward hacks and number-sequence fine-tunes are not reported as tests of broad misalignment.
No in-context examples of the narrow harmful tasks are tested for causing broad misalignment.
No reinforcement-learning intervention is tested for causing broad misalignment.
No shared direction or persona feature is tested as a mediator across fine-tunes.

The study does not test requested-bad-behaviour framing or benign retraining after an induced misalignment effect. Benign verse datasets are compared as fine-tuning conditions, not as post-effect remediation.

The study uses four seeds and coherent-answer filtering, and compares 8B and 13B models and several post-training conditions. It does not sweep model scale broadly or measure the effect across intermediate training checkpoints.
